lesson.title: Mapping Every Possible Outcome: The Sample Space
lesson.summary: The sample space is the complete, carefully built list of every outcome a random phenomenon can produce, and it has to be right before any probability can be calculated from it.
lesson.body:
A sample space is the complete list of every possible outcome a random phenomenon can produce, usually written as S. It is the stage on which every probability question is asked, and it has to be built correctly before any probability can be calculated, because a probability is ultimately just a way of measuring how much of the sample space a particular event covers. An event, as covered earlier, is simply any subset of the sample space, any collection of outcomes a person might care about, such as rolling an even number or a survey respondent answering yes. Sample space comes first because you cannot define which outcomes count as a given event until you know the full universe of outcomes the event is being carved out of.

Sample spaces can be described in several ways depending on the phenomenon. For something simple like a single die roll, a plain list works: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. For a sequence of steps, like flipping a coin and then rolling a die, a tree diagram is often clearer, branching first into heads or tails and then into each of the six die faces from each branch. For two simultaneous random phenomena, like rolling two dice at once, a two way table with one die's faces along the rows and the other's along the columns lays out all 36 combinations at a glance. The right tool depends on the situation, but the goal is always the same: make sure every possible outcome appears exactly once, with nothing missing and nothing double counted.

Building the sample space correctly matters because a subtle miscount changes every probability calculated afterward. A common error is failing to account for order when it matters, such as treating heads then tails as the same outcome as tails then heads when the actual phenomenon distinguishes the sequence. Another common error is assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not, such as treating the sum of two dice as if all eleven possible sums from 2 to 12 were equally probable, when in fact a sum of 7 has far more ways to occur than a sum of 2.

Consider flipping a fair coin twice. The sample space has four outcomes, each equally likely because the coin is fair and the two flips do not influence each other: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, and each outcome has probability one fourth. Define event A as at least one head appearing across the two flips. Checking the sample space, A contains three of the four outcomes, HH, HT, and TH, leaving only TT outside of A. Since these three outcomes are disjoint, meaning no single flip sequence can simultaneously be HH and HT, the addition rule allows their probabilities to be summed directly: P(A) = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. As a check, the complement of A is simply TT, with probability 1/4, and 1 minus 1/4 equals 3/4, confirming the answer two different ways.

Everything in the next several chapters depends on this foundation. Knowing exactly what the complement of an event looks like, and whether two events share any outcomes at all, only makes sense once the full sample space they are both carved out of has been laid out clearly.
